newsitem.title: USA: Clinton meets mayors on welfare, makes no promises.
newsitem.headline: Clinton meets mayors on welfare, makes no promises.

text.p: President Clinton Wednesday met 14 mayors to discuss urban issues, chiefly the welfare reform law, but made no commitments on how the federal government may help cities cope with the legislation.

The mayors told reporters after the meeting, which lasted about an hour and included Vice President Al Gore and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, that the president had heard them out but made no promises.

"We can't do real welfare reform on the cheap," said Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell. "If we all believe people shouldn't receive welfare, that they should go out and work, then we've got to create employment opportunities."
Rendell said Clinton listened to the mayors, who are worried the law will push people off public assistance without jobs to go to, but offered "no firm commitments on anything."

"We are in the middle of the budget process," said a White House spokeswoman. "The president was happy to listen to their suggestions and will take them into consideration as we work through the budget process."

In August Clinton signed a welfare reform law that ended the 61-year-old federal guarantee of aid to the poor, giving states broad power to design their own welfare programs and limiting public assistance to five years.
Clinton has pledged to seek changes in some aspects of the law, including provisions that impose cuts on the Food Stamps program and that cut off aid to legal immigrants.
As part of the budget process, officials have said Clinton was studying the possibility of restoring roughly one quarter of the $55 billion in spending cuts called for in the law.

"The president indicated that he is going to be pushing for some changes in welfare," Fort Wayne, Indiana Mayor Paul Helmke told reporters after meeting Clinton. "These folks are going to start showing up on our doorsteps."
